The horn itself forms the main resonating cavity, its natural interior ground and hollowed out to make the bore. The mouthpiece is of horn or wood; the simplest versions sound through the natural opening at the tip, while improved models carry a clarinet-like reed device made of wood or bone. The instrument keeps the original shape and texture of the horn, with no modern metal or synthetic treatment.

It was mostly heard in the high summer pastures, where shepherds and dairymaids used it to signal, to manage the herd or to drive off predators. The important change came when fingerholes were cut into it, which let it play melodies, unlike an ordinary ram's horn, and turned it into a performing instrument. The way of blowing it also developed from the common brass-style mouthpiece to a clarinet-like single-reed version. Modern players include Karl Seglem and Sissel Morgan Gullou, the latter of whom has played on an animated film score, which shows the instrument continuing from a pasture tool onto the stage and into film music.

Its range is fairly narrow, mostly in the low and middle register; it is not especially loud, but it carries well. The sound comes from the natural resonance inside the horn, and each horn differs with the thickness and shape of its material, so each has a clear character of its own. Compared with modern brass it lacks metallic brilliance and is closer to the warmth of the raw animal horn; compared with woodwinds its tone is rougher and less tamed, full of the bleakness of old pastures, with a distinctive folk flavour and a sense of history.

The bukkehorn (Norwegian: Bukkehorn, Swedish: bockhorn) is an ancient Scandinavian aerophone, Hornbostel-Sachs classification number 423.1. It is made from the horn of a goat or a ram, the horn usually being worked five to seven years after it is taken; some versions have fingerholes cut in them and can play melodies. Traditionally it was used by shepherds and dairymaids in the high summer pastures, as a tool for signalling, managing the herd or driving animals off. It is usually played with a brass-style embouchure, sounding by the vibration of the lips, and there are also versions that use a single reed.
